title.en: The Buddha's Awakening and Great Passing Away
title.zh: 佛陀之成正覺與大般涅槃

region.zh: 印度菩提伽耶與拘屍那揭羅

texts.period: Canonical texts c. 4th-2nd c. BCE (oral transmission); written Pali canon in Sri Lanka 1st c. BCE; principal MS tradition: Pali script MSS, e.g. Brunet? (PTS editions); Mahaparinibbana Sutta (DN 16)

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (Rhys Davids translations) / SuttaCentral.net
source.work: Majjhima Nikaya 26 (Ariyapariyesana Sutta); Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), trans. T. W. Rhys Davids, Dialogues of the Buddha, PTS, 1899-1921

summary.en: The ascetic Siddhattha leaves his palace, studies under two teachers, rejects their paths, and attains awakening under the Bodhi tree; forty-five years of teaching later, he dies at Kushinagar between two sala trees, is cremated like a world-monarch, and his relics are divided into eight portions — nirvana beyond rebirth.
summary.zh: 悉達多太子捨家出家，從二師學而棄其道，於菩提樹下成正覺；說法四十五載，於拘屍那揭羅雙娑羅樹間大般涅槃，以轉輪王法焚身，舍利分作八份——此為解脫輪迴之涅槃敘事。

sensitivity.note: Canonical scripture of a living tradition (Pali canon); Vesak and relic cults treat these sites as sacred.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of MN 26: The ascetic Siddhattha, having studied under Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta and found their attainments short of the deathless, recalls the bliss of the first meditation he knew as a child under the rose-apple tree: 'Might this be the path to awakening?' and, taking solid food, sits down to strive. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of MN 26; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of DN 16: The Buddha lies between two sala trees at Kusinara; the twin trees flower out of season and celestial music sounds; he tells Ananda: 'It may be that ye think... the Master is gone. But thus should ye think: the Doctrine and the Discipline he has made known — that is your Master when I am gone.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of DN 16; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: T. W. Rhys Davids, Dialogues of the Buddha (PTS, 1899-1921, public domain); modern: Bhikkhu Bodhi (copyright)

narrative.en:
The two canonical poles of the Buddha's biography — the night of awakening and the great passing — bracket forty-five years of ministry and together constitute the charter narrative of the Buddhist path.

THE GOING FORTH. The Pali canon tells the renunciation briefly (MN 26, MN 36), expanding it in the commentarial Nidanakatha. Prince Siddhattha Gotama of the Sakyans, son of Suddhodana, lives a palace life of the three mansions until the sight of the four signs — an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a renunciate — convicts him of aging, sickness, and death. He leaves Kapilavatthu by night, casts off his hair, and dons ochre robes; his son is born that same night and he names him Rahula, 'the fetter' — and leaves anyway: 'A fetter has been born.'

THE SEARCH AND THE AWAKENING. He studies first under Alara Kalama (attaining the 'sphere of nothingness'), then Uddaka Ramaputta (the 'sphere of neither perception nor non-perception') — and rejects both: 'This doctrine does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace... to nirvana.' He joins the five ascetics at Uruvela and undertakes extreme austerities for six years, to the point of skeleton-like self-mortification, and rejects this too, recalling the spontaneous bliss of the first meditation he had known as a child under the rose-apple tree — 'might this be the path to awakening?' — and takes milk-rice offered by the village girl Sujata. Seated on a mat of grass under the Bodhi tree (pipphali), he makes the vow not to rise until liberation. Mara, the tempter, challenges his seat-right: 'Who is thy witness?' — the Buddha touches the earth, and the earth goddess (in the later account) roars in witness. Mara's armies of desire, aversion, and doubt are defeated; through the three watches of the night the Buddha attains the three knowledges — his own former lives, the passing and arising of all beings according to karma, and the destruction of the cankers (asava) — 'birth is destroyed... this is the last birth; there is now no renewed existence'. The awakening formulas of dependent arising (paticca-samuppada) are recited three times in the canonical account.

THE MINISTRY AND THE GREAT PASSING. He teaches for forty-five years (his first sermon at Sarnath, 'the wheel of dhamma', sets the path rolling). At eighty, on his final journey, he is poisoned by Cunda the smith's 'pig's delight' (sukara-maddava) — he foretells it, takes on the suffering, and walks to Kusinara. There, between two sala trees, he lies on his right side 'like a lion': the trees flower out of season and celestial music honors him; his disciple Subhadda becomes the last convert. Ananda grieves; the Buddha consoles him ('all that is dear is subject to change') and lays down the succession: 'the Doctrine and the Discipline... that is your Master when I am gone' (DN 16). He asks the assembly three times whether any has a doubt — silence. 'Now then, monks, I say to you: all conditioned things are subject to decay. Strive on with diligence!' (vayadhamma samkhara, appamadena sampadetha) — and he passes from the fourth meditation to nirvana without remainder (anupadisesa-nibbana). The Mallas cremate him with royal rites like a world-monarch; the relics are claimed by eight kingdoms and divided into eight portions (a war of relics is averted by the brahmin Drona), each enshrined in a stupa — the aition of the stupa cult.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds the Buddhist analysis of suffering and liberation (the four signs as the problem; the awakening as the solution), the middle way between indulgence and self-torment (the milk-rice episode), the sanctity of the sites (Bodh Gaya, Kusinagar — among the eight great pilgrimage places), Vesak (the full-moon festival of birth, awakening, and passing), and the relic-stupa economy that structures Buddhist devotional space; the succession formula grounds the sangha's authority in dhamma-vinaya rather than a living teacher.
narrative.zh: 悉達多太子因四門遊觀見老病死與沙門，捨家夜遁，剃髮披衣，名子羅睺羅為『繫縛』。先從阿羅邏迦蘭學無所有處定，從鬱陀迦羅摩子學非想非非想定，皆棄之，言其道不至涅槃；六年苦行形同枯骨，亦棄之，憶幼時閻浮樹下初禪之樂，受牧羊女乳糜，於畢缽羅樹下敷草而坐，誓不證無上正覺不起。魔羅譏其座位無證，佛觸地為證，魔軍潰敗；夜三時得三明：宿命、天眼見眾生業報流轉、漏盡——『生已盡，梵行已立，所做已辦，不受後有』。說法四十五年，初轉法輪於鹿野苑。八十歲末行，受鐵匠純陀供養而中毒，行至拘屍那揭羅，於雙娑羅樹間右脅如獅子臥；樹非時開花，天樂供養；化度末化者須跋陀羅；阿難憂泣，佛慰之：『諸行無常，法與律為汝等師。』三問眾無疑，末誡：『諸行無常，精進勿懈！』入第四禪而般涅槃。諸末羅以轉輪王法焚身，舍利八分起塔供養——塔制之緣起。功能：苦與解脫之釋義、中道之範、八大聖地朝聖、衛塞節、以及僧團依法不依人之憲章。

functions: Charter of the middle way: rejection of both palace indulgence and mortification
Pilgrimage geography: Bodh Gaya, Kusinagar among the eight great sites; Vesak festival
Stupa cult: relic division into eight portions grounds devotional architecture
Sangha authority: dhamma-vinaya as the Master after the passing

variants.name: Nidanakatha (commentarial biography)
variants.text_tradition: Introductory narrative of the Jataka commentary (Buddhaghosa, 5th c. CE)
variants.summary: Supplies the palace drama the canon omits: the four signs, Yasodhara, Kanthaka the horse, the gate-gods lifting the prince over the city — the biography most people know, transmitted as comment rather than sutta.

variants.name: Sarvastivada/Lalitavistara tradition
variants.summary: A hagiographic expansion (Buddha's birth from his mother's side, the seven steps, mara's daughters) that fed Mahayana devotional art from Gandhara to Dunhuang; the awakening is a cosmic event witnessed by all beings.

variants.name: Mahaparinibbana doublet verses
variants.summary: The passing-away sutta preserves older verse doublets (e.g. the 'earthquake' verses) whose repetitions betray a centuries-long oral transmission before the 1st-c. BCE writing down in Sri Lanka.

title.en: The Transformations of Lord Lao: Laozi's Hagiography in Daoist Tradition
title.zh: 太上老君變化紀：道教老子聖傳

region.en: Louguan (Louguantai), Shaanxi, China (the western pass; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中國陝西樓觀台（西出函谷關；象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hagiographic strata: Shiji 63 (c. 90 BCE); Laozi bianhua jing (Scripture of the Transformations of Laozi, Dunhuang MS, 6th-9th c. CE); Shenxian zhuan (c. 4th c. CE)

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (Dao De Jing translations) / Daozang (DZ 1412 etc.)
source.work: Laozi bianhua jing (Scripture of the Transformations of Lord Lao, DZ 1412?); Sima Qian, Shiji 63; Ge Hong, Shenxian zhuan (trans. R. F. Campany, To Live as Long as Heaven and Earth, 2002)

texts.license: Ancient texts public domain; Campany 2002 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: The Dao itself takes embodied form: Laozi is born of a plum tree under his mother's left armpit after eighty-one years in the womb, serves as Zhou court archivist, transmits the five-thousand-character scripture to Yin Xi at the western pass, and through eight incarnations teaches the world until the Daoist empire of the Tang crowns him 'August Emperor of the Mysterious Origin'.
summary.zh: 大道化身：老君自母左腋下李樹而出，懷胎八十一年；為周守藏室之史，於函谷關授關令尹喜五千言；歷八十一變教化世間，至唐代李氏尊為『太上玄元皇帝』。

sensitivity.note: Daoist scriptural canon (Daozang) is sacred to a living tradition; these hagiographic narratives are public liturgical culture. Ordination-restricted liturgies are not reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Shiji 63 (Sima Qian, c. 90 BCE): Laozi was a man of Quren village in Li township of Ku county in Chu; he served the Zhou court as archivist; seeing the decline of Zhou, he departed westward; at the pass, the keeper Yin Xi asked him to write a book — Laozi composed a work in two parts, on the Way and its power, five thousand characters and more, and went off; no one knows where he died. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Shiji 63 (Sima Qian, c. 90 BCE); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Laozi bianhua jing: Lord Lao declares: 'I have no fixed form; in response to beings I transform.' He lists his embodiments — in the age of the Three Kings and Five Emperors as teacher of rulers, as personal savior in each dynasty — and foretells the age when Li Hong, the 'heir of the Dao', will descend to gather the elect and bring the world of Great Peace. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Laozi bianhua jing; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Primary texts public domain; scholarly translations: Livia Kohn (The Taoist Experience, 1993; God of the Dao, 2000) and R. F. Campany (2002) — quoted only as summary

narrative.en:
Daoism did not merely preserve a philosopher: it developed a full hagiography in which the historical Laozi (traditionally Li Er, court archivist of Zhou, 6th-4th c. BCE) is an incarnation of the Dao itself — Lord Lao (Taishang Laojun), second in the Daoist trinity after the Celestial Worthy and before the Celestial Master.

THE HISTORICAL SKELETON. Sima Qian's Shiji 63 (c. 90 BCE) gives the oldest account: Laozi of Chu served as archivist of the Zhou archives; seeing Zhou's decline, he departed west; at the pass, the keeper Yin Xi begged him to write; Laozi composed the two-part 'Way and Power' text of over five thousand characters and vanished, 'no one knows where he died'. Confucius' legendary visit ('a dragon... I cannot know') is attached; Sima Qian already notes rival claims (Lao Laizi; the Daoist Grand Historian of Duke Xian) — the ambiguity that later hagiography resolved by making multiplicity essential: the sage has no single body.

THE MIRACULOUS BIOGRAPHY. The Shenxian zhuan (Ge Hong, c. 4th c.) and the Laozi bianhua jing build the deity: Laozi's mother, pregnant for eighty-one years, gives birth from her left armpit under a plum tree (li — his surname); the infant walks immediately, points to the plum tree, and has white hair and long ears ('Laozi' — 'Old Child'). He serves the declining Zhou; the world decays around him; he rides a green ox west, and at the Hangu Pass Yin Xi — himself a visionary who reads the breath of the east as 'purple vapor from ten thousand li, a sage coming' — receives the five thousand characters of the Daode jing and the transmission of the Dao. Laozi's later career is a trajectory of epiphanies: at Louguan (the 'Look-at-the-Terrace' hermitage founded on the spot), he reveals the Xisheng jing ('Scripture of Western Ascension'); in the Zhang Lu tradition, Lord Lao descends in 142 CE to Mount Heming and consecrates Zhang Daoling as Celestial Master, founding organized Daoism — the hagiographic hinge between philosopher and church.

THE TRANSFORMATIONS AND THE MESSIANIC END. The bianhua tradition lists Lord Lao's cyclic incarnations: in every age of the Three Kings and Five Emperors he appears as teacher and regenerator of rulers; under the Shang and Zhou he descends as savior 'nine times nine' — the scripture says he 'was never born, yet manifests birth; never dies, yet manifests passing'. The eschatological horizon is Li Hong (the 'heir'), the future Lord Lao who will descend at the world's crisis to gather the righteous and establish Great Peace (taiping) — a millenarian expectation that repeatedly ignited Daoist uprisings across the medieval period. The imperial cult completed the arc: the Tang dynasty (Li family, 618-907) claimed Laozi as ancestor, erecting steles at Louguan and conferring the title 'August Emperor of the Mysterious Origin' (Taishang Xuanyuan Huangdi, 666 CE) — the sage becomes the empire's ancestor-god, and his cult at Louguan, Wudang, and the Baiyun guan anchors Daoist liturgy to this day.

FUNCTIONS. The hagiography grounds Daoist liturgy (the Three Pure Ones' throne; the audience with Lord Lao in jiao offerings), legitimizes the lineage (Zhang Daoling's revelation; the Louguan tradition), aitiologizes the Daode jing as revealed scripture rather than composed book, and structures Daoist messianism (Li Hong; taiping).
narrative.zh: 太史公《史記》卷六十三記老子為楚苦縣厲鄉曲仁里人，周守藏室之史，見周衰西去，關令尹喜強而著書上下篇言道德之意五千餘言，莫知所終。後世道教聖傳層累：老君自母左腋生於李樹之下，懷胎八十一年，生而能行，白髮長耳，號『老子』；騎青牛西出函谷，紫氣東來，尹喜讀氣知聖人至，受五千言並受道訣；於樓觀說《西昇經》；漢安元年鶴鳴山降授張道陵天師之職，開教立治。《老子變化經》（敦煌本）言老君『隨時感化』，三皇五帝之世為帝王之師，商周以降九九化身，救度世人；末世將降李弘，收種民致太平。唐李氏尊為祖，封『太上玄元皇帝』，樓觀立碑。功能：齋醮科儀之供奉、道統之根、五千言為天啟之經、李弘彌賽亞主義。

functions: Legitimation of the Daoist lineage: Zhang Daoling's revelation at Mount Heming
Aition of the Daode jing as revealed scripture (five thousand characters at the pass)
Liturgical anchor: Lord Lao's throne in jiao offerings and the Three Pure Ones
Daoist messianism: Li Hong and the expectation of Great Peace (taiping)

variants.name: Shiji 63 (historiographic version)
variants.text_tradition: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian, c. 90 BCE
variants.summary: The sober oldest account, already noting rival identities (Lao Laizi; Zhou Grand Historian Tan) — later hagiography turns this very multiplicity into proof of the Dao's bodiless transformations.

variants.name: Laozi bianhua jing (Dunhuang recension)
variants.text_tradition: Dunhuang MS S.2295; scripture 6th-9th c. CE
variants.summary: First-person apocalypse: Lord Lao lists his incarnations 'nine times nine' and foretells Li Hong's descent; recovered at Dunhuang, it shows the messianic strand in full.

variants.name: Xisheng jing (Western Ascension)
variants.text_tradition: Scripture of Western Ascension, Louguan tradition, 5th-6th c.
variants.summary: Laozi's discourse to Yin Xi after crossing the pass — the 'westernization' strand (huahu) later used to claim Laozi taught the Buddha, a polemic that shaped Sino-Buddhist debate.

variants.name: Tang imperial cult
variants.text_tradition: Imperial steles at Louguan (e.g. 626, 666 CE); Daozang liturgies
variants.summary: The Li family claims Laozi as ancestor; imperial jiao sacrifices crown the sage as 'August Emperor' — the hagiography becomes state religion, with steles and images across the empire.
